title: The forest of knowledge under global change.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: I opened the real files. The main database (Camara-Leret_2026_The-Forest-of-Knowledge.csv, 52,013,831 bytes) sits first inside an 11 GB Zenodo zip, so rather than breach the 50 MB download rule I read the zip's central directory with HTTP range requests and pulled only that entry's 2.86 MB compressed slice (~8.6 MB downloaded in total). Verified myself: 90,536 data rows and 41 columns, every one of the 90,537 lines having exactly 41 fields, parsing under strict UTF-8 with no errors; 700 unique references; 7,578 unique resolved species names, 1,791 genera, 247 families; 12 use categories (Medicine 42,160, HumanFood 14,360, Construction 9,011); 25 plant parts; 754 composite 'part_category_subcategory' strings; 167 Glottolog language codes present (35,112 rows blank, 39%); latitude missing in 96.6% of rows; Ref_year running 1504-2023 with 27,013 reports from pre-2000 references. I reproduced the paper's published numbers: applying the authors' own documented filter analyze_amazon_v2 != 'n' (confirmed as the filter used, by reading their R code) gives exactly 5,796 utilised species, and reference counts for the five most-cited species came out exactly as published (178, 176, 165, 148, 120). I also opened Supplementary Table 2 (4.0 MB xlsx): 17,376 rows, 47 columns, with a 'useful' column of 6,425 ones and 10,951 zeros, plus World Checklist of Vascular Plants IDs and synonym status. And amz_species_resolved_taxonomy.csv (range-downloaded, 241,653 bytes): 8,497 species with a two-value 'aups' label, 4,522 TRUE / 3,960 FALSE / 15 NA. I computed first-documentation year per species myself: 1,826 labelled-used species first appear in references from 2000 onward.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Only read, not checked in files: that the species distribution models cover 8,429 species under three climate scenarios; the projected 28-34% local loss of utilised species and the 26% knowledge-pool reduction from threatened languages; the modelling workflow described in the ODMAP supplementary note. I deliberately did not download AUPS_Wallace_p10.zip (10,993,784,022 bytes of distribution-model rasters) - I recorded its size from the zip directory only. I also did not verify the paper's 'Indigenous groups' per-species counts: my naive count of the tribe columns gave 65 groups for Bactris gasipaes where the paper says 58, so their group definition applies a filter I did not replicate.

a1_downloadable.note: Zenodo record 19202485 is open with no login and licensed CC BY 4.0. I fetched real bytes from it. The 11 GB bundling is awkward but Zenodo honours HTTP range requests (confirmed: 206 Partial Content), so the useful tables come down in megabytes. The companion website is an interactive browser app with no bulk download.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The label is literally a column, in two places I opened: 'aups' (TRUE/FALSE, used by people or not) in a two-column CSV of 8,497 species, and 'useful' (1/0) in Supplementary Table 2. Nothing has to be constructed. A link-prediction variant (does culture X use plant Y) would instead need negatives built from unobserved cells, so I did not make that the primary task.

a3_inputs_present.note: Features are in the files as values, not as accession numbers: family, genus, resolved species name, country, plant part, language code, reference year. Species range-size features sit in a separate 16 MB CSV in the same deposit. No external lookups needed for the primary task.

a4_units_stated.note: The label is a yes/no flag, so units do not apply, and there is no hidden scale to get wrong. The supporting range-area table is in stated area units; the use categories follow a published classification standard the same group helped revise.

a5_enough_rows.note: Counted by me: 90,536 use records. The modelling unit is the species, and there are 8,482 species with a non-missing yes/no label (4,522 used, 3,960 not), far above the ~1,500 threshold and unusually well balanced.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Skipping the 11 GB raster archive, every table I need totals about 100 MB uncompressed (52 MB main database, 24 MB use-category areas, 16 MB range statistics, 7 MB knowledge join, 4 MB checklist). Peak memory around 2 GB. The baseline is a tree model on 8,482 rows: no graphics card needed.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Checked and reconciled, which is the strongest thing here. 90,536 records and 700 references match exactly, and the authors' documented filter column reproduces their headline 5,796 utilised species exactly. Per-family counts differ from Extended Data Fig. 7 because that figure covers only the distribution-modelled subset - explicable, so I can tell which number is which.

a8_label_provenance.note: The label traces to a human-curated reading of 700 published ethnographic and botanical references, not to any model output, and is not computable from the features. One real trap sits nearby: the climate range-change outcomes ARE species-distribution-model predictions, so using those as a label would be circular. I excluded them. Separate caveat for Part H: 'not used' really means 'not yet documented as used'.

B1.why: Label in a 2-column CSV, features across 2-3 more; species-name key joins (4,678 of 8,497 overlap, checked in files)

B2.why: Strict UTF-8 parse succeeded; all 90,537 lines have exactly 41 fields; xlsx opened first try

B3.why: One binary label definition applied by authors across all 700 references; use categories follow a published standard

B4.why: No censored labels, but native_resolved is messy free text (206 value combinations) and coordinates 96.6% missing; checked in file

B5.why: Supp Table 2 has 17,376 rows for 16,221 species; 1,463 synonyms flagged, and accepted-ID column makes dedupe easy

B6.why: Column names self-describing and R code reveals filter logic, but no data dictionary for analyze_amazon_v2, rcl_add, taxonomic_verification codes

C1.why: Asks how far documented use predicts newly documented use; a low score is itself the finding about fieldwork bias

C2.why: 4 searches found no model for this task; nearest (Howes 2023) predicts lab antimalarial activity on 282 species

C3.why: Dataset built for climate/language accounting, not prediction; Amazonian Indigenous knowledge underrepresented versus Kew's three-family work

C4.why: Alternative is multi-year ethnographic fieldwork with communities plus lab screening; 700 references took decades to accumulate

C5.why: Obvious dummies: 53% base rate, per-genus rate, range-size-only. Howes 2023 published precision 0.67 as a reference point

D1.why: No sequences, structures, molecules or cells in the files; none of ESM-2, ChemBERTa, DNABERT, scGPT fits a plant-use table

D2.why: Nothing to freeze; baseline is a from-scratch tree model. A chemistry route needs an external database, breaking A3

D3.why: CC BY 4.0 on the Zenodo deposit and the article, confirmed in the record metadata; fully permissive

E1.why: Three leakage-free splits available: held-out language, held-out plant family, and reference-year temporal; all columns verified present

E2.why: Counted in file: 64 of 167 languages have 50+ records, plus 247 plant families and 700 references as alternative groups

E3.why: Global base rate 4,522/8,482 = 53%, per-genus rate, and range-size-only logistic regression; all computable from files

E4.why: Unusually estimable: the temporal split directly measures the documentation miss rate (1,826 of 5,811, computed by me)

E5.why: Palms must rank top: I reproduced the published reference counts for all five most-cited species exactly (178/176/165/148/120)

E6.why: Label shuffle must collapse to the 53% base rate; within-genus shuffle tests the grouped split; noise features as control

E7.why: Ref_year column present and verified (1504-2023, 27,013 pre-2000 reports), so a temporal split costs one line

E8.why: Already reproduced three published numbers from the file (90,536 records, 700 references, 5,796 utilised species) using authors' R code

G1.why: Standard IDs present in files: Glottolog codes (168), ISO 639-3 (165), World Checklist of Vascular Plants and IPNI IDs

G2.why: GBIF, the ~3-billion-record occurrence database, joins on the accepted species name / WCVP taxon ID already in Supp Table 2

G3.why: Species-to-many-occurrences collapses cleanly to a record count; synonyms resolvable via the wcvp_accepted_id column I saw

G4.why: Separates real cultural selection from collection effort - neither dataset can do that alone

H1.why: 3,960 species labelled not-used, but these are undocumented rather than tested; the temporal split quantifies the gap at ~31%

H2.why: 700 independent references, 9 countries, 167 languages, 247 families, though Ecuador is 30% of records (counted in file)

H3.why: Statable in one sentence: predicts documentation of use by a given date, not usefulness; see honest_claim_h3

H4.why: Paper explicit about language threat and under-documentation, but the 96.6% missing coordinates and Ecuador skew only visible in the file

I1.why: Named: the Camara-Leret lab (Zurich), Kew's medicinal plants group (Howes et al.), Conservation International's Moore Center (co-author)

I2.why: A measured documentation-versus-biology gap would redirect which regions get fieldwork and which species get screened

I3.why: Decision is which species to survey or screen, so precision at top-k is the metric - the same one Howes et al. argue for

I4.why: Honest risk: per-genus base rate plus range size may capture most signal, making this a short note rather than a model

J1.why: Real modelling with grouped and temporal splits and positive-unlabelled learning, but no pretrained-backbone transfer learning

J2.why: Plant taxonomy and Amazonian ethnobotany are specialist, but the palm positive control makes nonsense detectable

J3.why: The cleaned species table with first-documentation year, and the measured ~31% documentation miss rate, stand alone as results

J4.why: No week count set; feature engineering on external occurrence data is an open-ended surface

J5.why: No kill date or condition written in NOTES.md; one line would fix this

existing_models.name: Howes et al. 2023, 'Machine learning enhances prediction of plants as potential sources of antimalarials' (Frontiers in Plant Science, doi 10.3389/fpls.2023.1173328, PMC10248027) - I retrieved and read the full text
existing_models.score_and_split: Support Vector classifier reached mean precision 0.67 in their bias-corrected setting, against 0.46 for the best selection rule based on traditional use alone. The split was 10 iterations of 10-fold stratified cross-validation, i.e. random, not grouped, and the training set was only 282 labelled species (132 active, 150 inactive) out of 21,111. Code and trait data archived at Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7836732.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Three things, stated plainly in their discussion: the models 'must be tested on the underlying population in order to obtain a true measure of model performance'; 282 labelled species is too small a training set; and 'it is difficult to ascertain with confidence which plants are inactive' - exactly the absence-of-evidence problem this Amazonian dataset has, but which this dataset can actually measure using its publication-year column.

backbone.name: None. This is the candidate's defining weakness. The data is a species-by-culture table of recorded plant uses with taxonomy, geography and language metadata - there are no protein or DNA sequences, no chemical structures, no single-cell profiles. So ESM-2 (a protein language model), ChemBERTa (molecules), DNABERT-2 or AlphaGenome (DNA) and scGPT (single cells) all simply do not apply. The honest baseline is gradient-boosted trees on taxonomy and range features, trained from scratch, which is cheap but is not transfer learning. One conditional route exists: join species names to LOTUS, an open natural-products database, pull the chemical structures of each plant's known compounds, and embed them with ChemBERTa - but those structures are not in these files, so it needs thousands of external lookups with unknown coverage for Amazonian plants, which fails the 'inputs present' killer for the primary task.
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU only; no graphics card needed at any stage
backbone.licence: CC BY 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution), on both the Zenodo deposit and the article - permissive, commercial use allowed with attribution

integration.partner_dataset: GBIF (Global Biodiversity Information Facility), the open occurrence database of roughly 3 billion specimen and observation records, used here as a measure of how much botanical collecting happened per species and per region
integration.join_key: Accepted species name plus the World Checklist of Vascular Plants identifier (wcvp_accepted_id), both of which I confirmed are already columns in Supplementary Table 2; its wcvp_status column flags the 1,463 synonyms so the collapse rule is 'map every name to its accepted identifier, then take one row per accepted species'
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does the recorded human use of an Amazonian plant reflect something about the plant itself, or mainly how much botanical and ethnographic fieldwork happened where it grows?

controls.positive_control: Two, both chosen in advance. First, palms must come out as the most-used lineage: the paper's five most-cited species are all palms, and I reproduced their reference counts exactly from the file (Bactris gasipaes 178, Oenocarpus bataua 176, Mauritia flexuosa 165, Euterpe precatoria 148, Iriartea deltoidea 120), so a model that does not rank palms highly is broken. Second, swap the real label for plant family and predict it from genus - that must come out near-perfect, or the plumbing is wrong.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the used/not-used label and confirm performance collapses to the 53% base rate. Shuffle within genus rather than globally, to confirm the grouped split is really grouping. Replace features with same-shape random noise and confirm it matches the dummy.
controls.external_validation: Best option is already in the file: the reference-year column (1504-2023) supports a prospective test - train only on what was documented before 2000, then check which of the then-undocumented species the 2000-2023 literature newly recorded as used. I counted 1,826 such new positives against 3,960 species still never documented. Secondary options: leave-one-reference-out across 700 independent references, and leave-one-language-out across 167 Glottolog codes. The same group's New Guinea dataset would be an ideal cross-continent test but its paper says additional data must be requested from the author, so it is not freely available.

honest_claim_h3: Given a plant's taxonomy and modelled geographic range, the model predicts whether that species had been documented as used by Amazonian peoples in the published literature by a given date - documentation, not usefulness. I measured why that distinction matters: of the species this framing would have called negative in 1999, about 31% (1,826 of 5,811) were documented as used in the following two decades.

pitch.headline: 90,536 hand-curated plant-use records from 700 references, with a ready-made yes/no label on 8,482 species and a 1504-2023 year column.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: I counted every headline number in the files themselves and they reproduce exactly — 90,536 records, 700 unique references, and the authors' own filter column yielding their published 5,796 utilised species — with the label sitting in a provided column, 4,522 used against 3,960 not, which is unusually balanced for a biology table, all under CC BY 4.0 in a ~100 MB working set. The comparable published effort here, Howes et al. 2023, had 282 labelled species; this has 8,482, and a reference-year column that lets you measure the unlabelled-positive rate those authors said they could not ascertain (that the labels come from a human reading of the 700 references rests on the paper's description, not on the files).
pitch.the_win: A prospective number, not a cross-validation number: train only on the 2,671 species documented as used before 2000, rank the remaining 5,811, and report precision at top-k against the 1,826 species that the 2000-2023 literature newly documented — anything well above the 31% base rate is a shortlist that demonstrably anticipates real discoveries. I counted those 1,826 held-out positives myself, so the test is known to be runnable before any modelling starts.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: A failed ranking is still the answer to the question, because the honest claim is about documentation rather than usefulness: if taxonomy, range and collecting effort cannot anticipate which species got recorded next, that tells shortlist-builders their lists are tracking fieldwork history, and if it can, it says the opposite. The one thing it will not teach is transfer learning — no pretrained backbone applies to this table, so the baseline is from-scratch gradient-boosted trees.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Zurich group that built this database, and the Kew medicinal-plant team behind the Howes et al. antimalarial work, both of whom already produce species shortlists. The decision it changes is which species they send people to survey in the field or screen in the lab.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a plant's taxonomy, geographic range and documentation history to predict whether Amazonian peoples are recorded using it.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is one Amazonian plant species, described by its botanical family and genus, its modelled geographic range, the countries it occurs in, and when it first appears in the literature. I verified 8,482 species carry a clean yes/no label, and 5,796 of them appear across 90,536 individual use records.
plain_idea.predict: The model outputs the probability that a species is recorded as used by people. The true answer comes from a hand-curated reading of 700 published ethnographic and botanical references, where each record names the plant part, the kind of use (medicine, food, construction and nine others) and the Indigenous group reporting it.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: The Zurich group that built this database, and Kew's medicinal-plant team who already build such shortlists, decide which species to survey in the field or screen in the lab. Showing how much of apparent 'usefulness' is really a record of where botanists happened to work would tell them whether their shortlists track biology or history - and that answer is useful whichever way it comes out.

ml_idea: Primary task: binary classification of Amazonian plant species as documented-as-used or not, from taxonomy (247 families, 1,791 genera), modelled range area, country occurrence and collection-effort features, with the label taken straight from the provided 'aups' column (4,522 used / 3,960 not). The experiment that matters is the prospective temporal test rather than ordinary cross-validation: fit on the 2,671 species documented as used before 2000, then score the remaining 5,811 and measure how well the ranking anticipates the 1,826 species that the 2000-2023 literature newly documented as used. Precision at top-k is the metric, because the real decision is which species to put on a field or screening shortlist. Secondary split: leave-one-language-out across 167 Glottolog codes, to ask how far one culture's plant knowledge predicts another's and whether accuracy decays with linguistic and geographic distance. This is a positive-unlabelled learning problem, and its value is that the data lets you estimate the unlabelled-positive rate directly instead of assuming it.

effort.compute_note: Partly timed, partly estimated. I actually parsed and profiled the 52 MB main database several times in this session with Python's standard library, and each pass took seconds, so the 2 GB peak-memory figure is a comfortable upper bound. The modelling table is only about 8,500 rows by a few dozen features, so a 10-fold grouped cross-validation of gradient-boosted trees is a couple of minutes. No model was trained and no embeddings are needed, since no pretrained backbone applies.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already done, and it passed. The check was a count: how many species inside the labelled set are first documented as used after 2000, since without enough of them the prospective test is impossible. Answer, computed from the file: 1,826 new positives against 3,960 species never documented as used. A few hundred would have been enough.

verdict_reason: The data is the cleanest I have verified against a paper: all eight killers pass with files actually opened, every headline number reproduces exactly (90,536 records, 700 references, and 5,796 utilised species via the authors' own documented filter and R code), the label is a provided column, the working set is about 100 MB, and the evaluation story is unusually strong - all eight Part E checks pass, including a prospective temporal test with 1,826 held-out positives that I counted myself, and a positive control (palms) whose published numbers I already reproduced. The question scores full marks because it cannot produce a useless answer. What stops it is Part D: there is no pretrained backbone for a table of plant uses. No sequences, no structures, no molecules, no cells, so ESM-2, ChemBERTa, DNABERT-2 and scGPT are all irrelevant, and the honest baseline is a from-scratch tree model. That scores 2 of 6 against a threshold of 4 and means the project would teach careful evaluation but not the transfer learning this search is for. Part J also falls short at 5 of 10, mostly for want of a written kill date. Park it as the strongest non-backbone candidate found so far, and promote it to 'do it' immediately if the backbone requirement is relaxed - on data quality and on question value it beats everything else evaluated. Secondary caution for whoever picks it up: the climate range-change outcomes in the same deposit are species-distribution-model predictions and must never be used as a label.
